120.title: Remembrance with breath
120.hook: simran is remembering the Name; here we let the breath carry it
120.howItsDone: Sikhs practice naam simran by repeating and meditating on the Name, often Waheguru, both in the early morning hours called amrit vela and in short moments throughout the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vand chakna: feeding one person, with no agenda. Your line was a small langar.

What do you carry everywhere without trying? Keys, most days. A phone, almost always. A worry or two. Every one of them has been left behind somewhere at least once: on a counter, in a cab, in a coat pocket. Except one. Your breath has never stayed home. It goes with you to the office, into the car, into a hospital bed, into sleep. It doesn't need a gurdwara or a book or a quiet room. On day fourteen, naam japna, keeping the name, was one of your first words. Now, a hundred and thirteen days later, the path comes back to it, slowly, for a whole week.
screen: `THE ONE THING YOU NEVER LEAVE BEHIND.` →`IT GOES WITH YOU EVERYWHERE.` → `BACK TO SIMRAN.`

segments.voice: Naam is the Name: not just a word for God, but God's presence, the truth the Name points to. Simran is remembering, from an old word meaning to call to mind. Naam simran: remembering the Name. It's the third pillar you met on day fourteen, naam japna, and Sikhs call it the heart of the whole path. Seva gets the hands ready. Kirtan gets the voice and the ear ready. Simran is where it all turns inward. Guru Arjan opens the Sukhmani, the hymn of peace, with it. In paraphrase: remember, keep on remembering, and find peace; the troubles of the body and the mind will leave. Again and again the Guru Granth Sahib pairs remembering with breathing. The Gurus speak of remembering God with every breath and every bite, so that no breath goes by empty. That's why this week joins simran to the breath. The breath is always there, so the remembering can always be there. It's slow, so it slows the mind. And it's honest: you can't breathe yesterday or tomorrow, only now. Some Sikhs sit for long hours of simran before dawn, in the time the Gurus called amrit vela, the ambrosial hours. Others remember in short moments through the day: at a red light, in a waiting room, before picking up the phone. Both are simran. No technique yet, no special words. Just the breath, and the Name held gently alongside it, however you understand it. Tomorrow, a way to give each breath its word.
screen: `NAAM AND SIMRAN.` · `THE THIRD PILLAR, TURNED INWARD.` · `REMEMBER, AND FIND PEACE.` · `WITH EVERY BREATH.` · then, large: `BREATH AND NAME.`

segments.voice: Sit upright with your hands resting and your eyes closed or soft, and just notice the breath, in and out; then let it slow a little, longer on the way in, longer on the way out. With each breath, let the Name be there in the background, the way a candle is there in a room. When your mind wanders, and it will, come back to the next breath.
Naam simran. Remembering the Name: the heart of Sikh practice, and this week, carried on the breath.
Your line: breath and name. The breath never stays home. One hundred twenty days now.

121.title: Wahe in, guru out
121.hook: many sound Wahe on the in-breath and Guru on the out-breath
121.howItsDone: Many Sikhs practice simran by silently sounding Wahe on the in-breath and Guru on the out-breath; others repeat Waheguru aloud or sing it together in kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, naam simran: remembering the Name, carried on the breath. Your line was breath and name.

Breathing is the one thing you do all day without ever deciding to, and almost none of those breaths get noticed. In, out, while you think about the email, the dishes, the thing somebody said at lunch. Now put a word on each breath. Not shouted, not even spoken. Just there, like a passenger. Many Sikhs do exactly this with one word, the word the Sikh code of conduct calls the Gurmantar. They split it in two. The first half rides in. The second half rides out.
screen: `BREATHS NOBODY NOTICES.` → `A WORD RIDING EACH ONE.` → `ONE WORD, SPLIT IN TWO.`

segments.voice: The word is Waheguru. You've met it already on this path: the Gurmantar, the Guru's own word for remembering God. Let's open it. Wahe is an exclamation of wonder, close to wow, the sound you make when a view stops you on a hill road. Guru means the teacher, the guide. So Waheguru is something like wonderful Teacher, a cry of wonder at the Divine. Now the breath. Many Sikhs practice simran by letting Wahe rise on the in-breath and Guru fall on the out-breath. The in-breath is the wonder, taking in. The out-breath is the Guru, letting go into trust. It's slow, and silent, or nearly so. Some say it quietly on the lips; some only in the mind. Others don't split the word at all, and repeat the whole of Waheguru aloud, in rhythm, or sing it in kirtan with the sangat. Sikh teachers and groups differ on the details, and the Guru Granth Sahib doesn't lay down a breathing method. What the hymns do say, over and over, is that a breath without the Name is wasted, and a breath with it is precious. So the breath isn't a trick. It's a clock you already carry, ticking whether you mean it to or not. Simran on the breath simply asks that some of those breaths remember where they came from.

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and take ten breaths this way: think Wahe slowly through the whole in-breath, and Guru all the way to the end of the out-breath, counting on your fingers if it helps. If you're here to learn rather than to pray, just listen to how the two halves feel different. After ten, let the words go and keep breathing.
Wahe in. The first half of Waheguru, the wonder, riding on the in-breath. Guru rides out.
Your line: wonder in, trust out. A cry of wonder, then a letting go. That's day one hundred twenty-one.

122.title: Satnam on the breath
122.hook: Sat on the inhale, Nam on the exhale
122.howItsDone: Satnam, from the opening line of the Guru Granth Sahib, is repeated in simran by some Sikhs, sometimes with Sat on the in-breath and Nam on the out-breath, and sometimes together with Waheguru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Waheguru split across the breath: Wahe in, Guru out. Your line was wonder in, trust out.

The people you love tend to have more than one name. The full name on the birth certificate. The nickname. The name only you use. Each one holds something different. The Guru Granth Sahib is like that about God. It uses many names, from many languages: Hari, Ram, Allah, Gobind, Prabhu, Kartar. But in the book's very first line there's a name that isn't really a name at all. It's a description. Two syllables, and it fits a breath exactly.
screen: `MANY NAMES FOR ONE YOU LOVE.` → `DOZENS OF NAMES FOR GOD.` → `ONE THAT FITS A BREATH.`

segments.voice: The Guru Granth Sahib opens with the Mul Mantar, the root verse. It begins with Ik Onkar, there is one God. The very next word is Satnam. Sat means true, real, what lasts. Nam means name. So Satnam is the true name, or better, the one whose name is truth. Here's the quiet surprise. Guru Nanak doesn't give God a proper name here. He gives a quality. Right after saying God is one, the text says God is real. Not a rumor, not a mood. True. Sikhs don't treat Satnam as a different God or a secret password. It's a way of naming the same One by what never changes. That's why it works so well as simran. Sat on the in-breath: the real, coming in. Nam on the out-breath: the name, going out into the day. Many Sikhs use Waheguru for simran, since that's the Gurmantar; some also breathe with Satnam, or say Satnam Waheguru together. Practices differ from sangat to sangat, and both words appear in the Guru Granth Sahib. You may have heard Satnam used as a greeting, or in yoga classes in the West. The everyday Sikh greeting is something else, Sat Sri Akal, but sat is in there too. Truth keeps turning up. Elsewhere in the Granth, Guru Nanak says truth is high, but higher still is truthful living. Satnam on the breath starts there: one real thing, noticed, again and again.

segments.voice: Ten breaths again, with the new word: let your shoulders drop, think Sat for the whole in-breath, and Nam all the way out. If you pray, let it be prayer; if you're here to learn, hear it as a plain word, true, name, and notice whether it feels different from yesterday's Wahe and Guru. Then just breathe.

123.title: When the mind runs off
123.hook: the hymns often call the mind restless; the practice is only to come back
123.howItsDone: Sikh teachers describe the wandering mind as the normal condition the hymns address, and simran as gently returning attention to the Name each time it drifts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satnam: Sat on the in-breath, Nam on the out. Your line was true name, breathing.

You sit down. You start the breath and the word. Wahe, Guru. Wahe, Guru. On the third breath you remember you never answered your sister's message. On the fourth you're planning dinner. By the sixth you're replaying an argument from 2019, and you've won it this time. Then, suddenly, you notice. Oh. I was supposed to be doing something. It's easy to read that moment as failure. The Gurus saw it very differently.
screen: `THE THIRD BREATH: A MESSAGE.` → `THE SIXTH: AN OLD ARGUMENT.` → `OH. I WANDERED.`

segments.voice: In Punjabi the mind is man, and the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib talk to it constantly, almost like a friend who won't sit still. They describe it running in all ten directions, chasing one thing after another, never staying in one place. The Gurus aren't surprised by this. They expect it. That's the first comfort: a wandering mind isn't a sign you're doing it wrong. It's the normal weather the hymns are written for. The second is how the Gurus speak to the mind. Not only with scolding. Guru Amar Das addresses it with astonishing tenderness. In paraphrase: O my mind, you are the very form of divine light; know where you came from. The restless thing that ran off to your 2019 argument is, in this line, made of light. It isn't the enemy. It's something that forgot its home. So the practice isn't chaining the mind down. It's only coming back. You notice you've wandered, and that noticing is itself the moment of simran. Then you return to the next breath and the word, without a lecture. Wander again in ten seconds? Come back again. A hundred times is fine. Simran is less like building a wall and more like calling a child home at dusk. You don't shout at the child for playing. You're just glad when they're back at the door.
screen: `MAN — THE MIND, RUNNING TEN WAYS.` · `THE GURUS EXPECT IT.` · `O MIND, YOU ARE FORMED OF LIGHT.` · `NOTICING IS THE SIMRAN.` · then, large: `COME BACK.`

segments.voice: Start with the breath and whichever word you like, Waheguru or Satnam, or just the breath if you'd rather. When your mind runs off, notice where it went, name it in one word, like work or food or worry, and come back to the next breath, kindly, the way you'd welcome that child home. See if you can come back three times.
Man. The Punjabi word for mind, which wanders in the hymns and is not scolded, only noticed, and brought back.

124.title: The early hours
124.hook: the ambrosial hours before dawn, praised in Japji's fourth pauri
124.howItsDone: Many Sikhs rise in the amrit vela, the hours before dawn, to bathe, recite the morning banis and do simran before the day's work begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, man: the mind that runs ten ways and is called home, not scolded. Your line was come back.

There's an hour most of us only meet by accident. The flight that leaves at six. The baby who won't settle. The night you couldn't sleep, finally gave up, and made tea. The house is silent. No messages, because everyone you know is asleep. Even the birds haven't started. It feels strange, a little lonely, and oddly clean. Sikhs have a name for that hour, and they don't treat it as an accident. They treat it as a gift, and some Sikhs set an alarm for it.
screen: `THE SIX O'CLOCK FLIGHT.` → `A SILENT HOUSE, NO MESSAGES.` → `AN HOUR WITH A NAME.`

segments.voice: The name is amrit vela. Vela means time, or hour. Amrit is nectar, the drink of immortality in old Indian stories, the thing that makes life deathless. So amrit vela is the nectar hour, often translated the ambrosial hour: the last watch of the night, before dawn. The text gives no clock time for it. It comes from Japji, Guru Nanak's morning hymn, the same fourth pauri where you met nadar, grace, on day one hundred eighteen. There he asks what we can offer to the One who gives everything, and answers: in the ambrosial hours, contemplate the true Name and its greatness. That's the whole instruction. No ritual, no list. Just the Name, in the early hour. Later, Guru Ram Das describes a Sikh's day, in paraphrase: one who calls himself a Sikh of the true Guru rises early and meditates on the Name, bathes, and keeps remembering through the day. Why so early? Sikh writers give a few reasons. The mind is quieter before the world starts pulling on it. The day hasn't made any claims yet, so the first thing it hears is the Name. And there's something honest about giving up a little sleep: it costs something. In many Sikh homes and gurdwaras the day really does begin this way, with Nitnem and simran in the dark, and at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar the Guru Granth Sahib is brought out in procession before dawn. Nobody has to become a monk to try it. Five minutes counts.

125.title: A string of beads
125.hook: some keep count of simran on a string of beads
125.howItsDone: Some Sikhs use a mala, often of wool or iron beads, to count repetitions of Waheguru during simran; many others do simran without one, and the Sikh code of conduct does not require it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amrit vela: the nectar hour before dawn, when the Name comes before anything else. Your line was the early hour.

Watch the hands of an older Sikh man at the back of a gurdwara, or a grandmother on a bus in Punjab. Sometimes a small loop of beads moves through the fingers, one at a time, while the lips move very slightly. No book open. No phone. Just thumb, bead, thumb, bead. Your grandparents may have done this too, in whatever tradition they came from: people all over the world have found that hands like having something to hold while the heart remembers.
screen: `A LOOP OF BEADS IN THE FINGERS.` → `THUMB, BEAD, THUMB, BEAD.` → `HANDS THAT HELP THE HEART.`

segments.voice: It's called a mala, which simply means a garland or a string. A Sikh mala is often made of wool, or of iron or steel beads, and many have one hundred and eight, though smaller ones are common too. Some Nihang Sikhs, the traditional warrior order in blue, wear large malas around the neck or wrist. The use is simple. With each bead, you say the Name once, usually Waheguru, and move on. The mala keeps count so the mind doesn't have to, and it gives restless fingers something to do. Here's the interesting part. The Guru Granth Sahib is honest that beads on their own do nothing. The Gurus and the saints in the Granth were sharp about outward show: counting beads for others to see while the heart is elsewhere. Kabir, one of the saints whose verses are in the Granth, turns the whole idea around. In paraphrase: my mala is my tongue, and the Name of the Lord is strung on it. The real string of beads is inside. So Sikhs hold the mala lightly. Many use one gladly as a help. Many never use one at all, and the Sikh code of conduct doesn't require it. Both are at home in the gurdwara. The point is never the count. Each bead is one more moment of remembering, and a hundred and eight small moments add up to something.

segments.voice: No beads needed: touch your thumb to each finger segment in turn, three segments on four fingers for twelve, then around again and a bit more, for twenty-seven, a quarter of a full mala. With each touch, say one word silently, Waheguru if you pray, or simply feel your breath if you'd rather. Lose count? Start again wherever you are.
Mala. A garland, a string of beads, often a hundred and eight, that some Sikhs use to count the Name.

126.title: Simran while working
126.hook: the Name can run quietly underneath ordinary work
126.carry: hands at work, heart at home
126.howItsDone: Many Sikhs keep up simran through the working day, quietly repeating Waheguru, listening to kirtan while they work, or pausing for a breath of remembering between tasks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mala: bead by bead, with the real string inside. And a week on the breath is nearly done: naam simran, Wahe in, Satnam, coming back, the early hour, the beads.
screen: `BREATH · WAHEGURU · SATNAM · COME BACK · AMRIT VELA · MALA.`

segments.voice: You can't sit with your eyes closed all day. There's a job. There are kids, a commute, a sink full of dishes, a shift that starts at seven. If remembering God only happens in the quiet corner before dawn, most of the day is left out. The Sikh Gurus were never monks. They farmed, traded, married and ran communities, so they had to answer this. Their answer is in a small, funny conversation between two saints.
screen: `YOU CAN'T SIT ALL DAY.` → `THE GURUS WERE NEVER MONKS.` → `A CONVERSATION BETWEEN TWO SAINTS.`

segments.voice: Among the short verses of Kabir in the Guru Granth Sahib, there's an exchange between two earlier saints of India, Trilochan and Namdev. Namdev was a cloth printer by trade, working with dyes all day. Trilochan teases him, in paraphrase: Namdev, you've been caught by the world. Why are you busy printing calico? Why not fix your mind on the Lord? Namdev answers, in paraphrase: with your mouth, keep the Lord's Name; with your hands and feet, do all your work; keep your consciousness with the Immaculate One. The work doesn't stop. The remembering doesn't stop. One runs underneath the other, like a song you hum while you cook. That fits the whole Sikh way of life. You've met the three pillars Sikhs trace to Guru Nanak: naam japo, remember the Name; kirat karo, earn an honest living; vand chhako, share. They sit side by side. For Sikhs, honest work isn't a distraction from the spiritual life. It's part of it. So what does it look like? For some, a quiet Waheguru under the breath while stacking shelves or driving. For others, a recording of kirtan playing while they work, or a single breath of remembering each time a task begins or ends. The hymns hold up remembering with every breath; in a working day, it's more like a home the heart can return to all day, while the hands stay busy.
screen: `TRILOCHAN TEASES NAMDEV.` · `HANDS AND FEET DO THE WORK.` · `REMEMBER, WORK, SHARE.` · `THE NAME RUNS UNDERNEATH.` · then, large: `HANDS AT WORK, HEART AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Stand up if you can and walk slowly, around the room, down a hallway or in place, letting each step land with a word: left foot, Wahe; right foot, Guru; or, if you'd rather, left foot, in-breath; right foot, out. Keep your eyes open: you're still in the world, doing something ordinary, with the remembering running underneath. When the mind wanders, come back.
Simran. The Name running quietly underneath ordinary work, as Namdev said: hands and feet at work, the heart with the One.
Your line: hands at work, heart at home. The dye and the Name, together, all day long. See you tomorrow.
